column41: The Southern Bell Frog, or Growling Grass Frog, (Litoria raniformis) occurs in south-eastern Australia, including Tasmania, and has been introduced into New Zealand.â¨The species prefers swamps, large dams or lagoons and other slow-moving or still bodies of water. Spawn is laid in floating clusters but may also be submerged and wrapped around aquatic plants; about 2400 eggs are laid in a clutch. The tadpoles take an average of 15 weeks to complete metamorphosis.â¨The maleâs call is made from among floating vegetation and on reeds near the water level, primarily after rain, from spring to autumn. The call has been described as a single drawn-out âcrawark-crawark-crok-crok.ââ¨Colouration varies, but is usually gold with large green blotches and spots; some individuals are almost all gold or all green. The back has wart-like bumps or protrusions.

column41: Sitting in a plant semi submerged in my pond. Approx 7 Cm in length.

Think it is the same individual that I photographed a couple of days back, in the same location in my backyard pond. Sitting motionless in sun and didn’t seem to be too frightened by camera closeups. Body approx 7 Cm long and 3-4 cm wide. Bright green with green and tan warty bumps on back and sides. Pale green stripe down its back. Looks to be pale under its chin. Black stripe marking from eyes to nostrils Very handsome frog.

column41: From: frogpole@tpg.com.au [mailto:frogpole@tpg.com.au]  Sent: Tuesday, 24 June 2014 4:59 PM To: Hope Ben Subject: Re: info on L raniformis   Hi Ben,   The sighting was in 2011. Here is all I have about the observation: The GPS I is 34 deg 36’ 19”S, 144 35’ 00.4”E (14 Feb 2011) from about 24-25 km SW Hay on the Balranald road (Sturt Hwy), in flooded grassland along long stretches of the northern side of the road (sounded like they extended for several hundred metres or more – maybe even a few kms). I didn’t get to see any frogs because the rotters disappeared underwater in the flooded grassland the moment you step into it at night, but there were large numbers calling spread out along this strip of road. The call was absolutely definitely this species (and the chorus almost deafening!).    The site is apparently flooded for some time when it does rain, because there were the typical taller emergent broader leaf water plants there that these frogs like, and lots of Marselia floating ever
